hero.name: Nikhil
hero.who: a 28-year-old solar pump founder in Nashik whose pitches leave farmers confused

story.h: Forty slides under a neem tree
story.b: Nikhil left an engineering job in Pune to start a small company that sells solar water pumps to farmers around Nashik. He knows the pumps inside out. At a village meeting near Sinnar, he stands under a neem tree with his laptop and presents forty slides: panel efficiency, controller specs, payback calculations. The farmers listen politely. One old man nods off. At the end nobody asks a single question, and the tea boy is the only one who takes a brochure. On the drive back, his co-founder Ashwini asks what the farmers will remember. Nikhil cannot answer. He explained everything perfectly. He is sure of it. So why did none of it stick?

ask.q: Nikhil explained his pump perfectly, yet nobody remembers anything. What should he work on?
o: Adding more data, so the farmers cannot argue
Shaping his message so listeners can grasp and remember it, not just so it is accurate
Speaking louder and with more energy
ask.why: Accuracy is not the same as being understood. More data buries the point deeper, and more energy cannot fix a message nobody can hold onto. Nikhil needs to shape his message around what the farmers will actually remember, and that is a skill he can learn.

chapters.take: An idea explained is not an idea understood. Make it stick.

story.b: On Sunday, Nikhil practises his pitch on his mother at the dining table in their flat on Nashik Road. She is a retired schoolteacher, sharp and patient. Within two minutes she stops him and asks what a kilowatt peak is. He opens his mouth and realises he has not thought about that question in years. It is so obvious to him that he forgot it was a question at all. He tries again, and she stops him at controller, then at payback period. Each time he has skipped a step that lives only in his head. By the end of the evening his notebook is full of words he must stop using, and his mother is pouring him a second cup of tea, amused.

ask.q: Ashwini is writing a training guide for new field staff and keeps using engineering terms. What should Nikhil suggest?
o: Add more technical detail, so the guide is complete
Assume new staff will pick up the terms on the job
Test it on a beginner, then drop jargon and fill in the skipped steps
ask.why: Once you know something well, it is hard to remember not knowing it. More technical detail deepens the problem, and assuming staff will pick it up is the same blind spot at work. Testing on a beginner shows Ashwini exactly where the gaps and jargon are.

chapters.take: What feels obvious to you is often a mystery to everyone else.

story.b: Nikhil spreads his forty slides on the floor as printouts and asks himself one question. If farmers remember only one thing, what should it be? Not panel efficiency. Not the warranty. After an hour of crossing things out, he arrives at it. Water whenever the crop needs it, with no diesel to buy. Everything else is detail. It feels almost too simple, as if he is throwing away years of engineering. But when he says it to Ganesh, their new field assistant and a farmer's son from Niphad, Ganesh repeats it back perfectly and adds that his father would understand it at once. Then Ashwini shows Nikhil her draft poster. It lists ten benefits in small print.

ask.q: Ashwini wants all ten pump benefits on the new poster. What should Nikhil suggest?
o: Pick the single most important point and say it plainly
Keep all ten, but use a smaller font so they fit
List them all, since farmers can choose what they like
ask.why: When ten points compete, none of them get remembered. A smaller font just hides them better, and a long list passes the hard work to the reader. Finding the one point that matters most and saying it plainly gives everyone one clear thing to carry home.

chapters.take: Find the one point that matters most, and say it so a child could repeat it.

story.b: At the next meeting, in a village near Dindori, Nikhil does not open his laptop. He places an empty yellow diesel can on the ground in front of the farmers and waits. People stop chatting. Then he asks how many times they filled a can like this last summer. A few farmers laugh and call out numbers. One man says he stopped counting. Nikhil asks a second question. What if it never needed filling again? Now everyone is leaning forward, waiting for the answer. He talks for only ten minutes after that, and three farmers ask for a visit. In the car, Ashwini says she will speak at a cooperative next week. She plans to begin with the company's history.

ask.q: Ashwini plans to open her cooperative talk with the company's history. What would grab attention better?
o: A joke about the weather to warm people up
A short question the farmers badly want answered, pointing to the main message
A longer history with more photos
ask.why: People tune out what they expect, and a company history is exactly that. A random joke grabs attention but leads nowhere. A question the farmers really want answered, pointing straight at the core message, opens a curiosity gap and keeps them listening for the answer.

chapters.take: Break the expected pattern, then make people curious about your core point.

story.b: Nikhil reads the new brochure Ashwini has drafted. It says their pump is a highly reliable, efficient and user-friendly solution. Every word is true, and none of them mean anything to a farmer standing in a dry onion field. He wonders what reliable actually looks like. So he visits Bhausaheb, one of their first customers near Niphad, and just watches. At sunrise the pump starts on its own. By eight in the morning, water has reached the last row of onions, before Bhausaheb's chai has gone cold. His teenage daughter switches it off with one button on her way to school. Nikhil writes all of it down in his notebook, word for word.

ask.q: The brochure calls the pump a highly reliable, efficient solution. How should Nikhil improve it?
o: Add more strong words like powerful and innovative
Keep it, since every company describes its products this way
Replace it with something farmers can picture, like water reaching the last row by eight
ask.why: Words like reliable and efficient slide off the mind because nobody can picture them. More strong words make it worse, and sounding like every other company makes Nikhil forgettable. A concrete image, like water reaching the last row by eight, sticks because everyone pictures the same thing.

chapters.take: Swap vague words for details people can see in their minds.

story.b: The district holds a big farm fair, and Nikhil gets five minutes on the main stage. He has a strong chart showing what customers saved on diesel, and he is proud of it. The night before, he thinks of Bhausaheb. Two summers ago, Bhausaheb's onion crop dried out when diesel ran short and the nearest fuel pump was shut. He borrowed money to replant. This summer, with the solar pump, his fields stayed green while neighbours queued for fuel. Bhausaheb told Nikhil, smiling, that he sleeps better now. Nikhil looks at his chart, then at his notes about Bhausaheb, and wonders which one the crowd will still remember tomorrow.

ask.q: Nikhil has only five minutes at the farm fair. What should he lead with?
o: Bhausaheb's story, told simply, with a number or two after it
A chart of average diesel savings across all customers
A list of every technical feature, to look serious
ask.why: People care about one person far more than about averages, and a feature list is easily forgotten. A simple story about Bhausaheb lets farmers picture themselves in his field, so they remember what changed and why it matters. A number or two afterwards gives them something to check.

chapters.take: People forget lists and charts, but remember a story about someone like them.

story.b: By spring, Nikhil's pitch has shrunk from forty slides to one yellow diesel can, one sentence and one story. He still knows every technical detail and shares it when farmers ask, which they now often do. His mother tests every new brochure before it goes to print, and she still stops him at any word she cannot picture. Ganesh tells Bhausaheb's story better than Nikhil does, and he has added a few of his own from Niphad. Ashwini's cooperative talk, which began with a question, brought in their first group order. They have hired two more field assistants. Nikhil still loves the engineering. He has simply learned that people must remember an idea before they can use it.

chapters.take: Simple, surprising, concrete and human. That is how an idea survives past lunch.
